summary: A BBN notice extending the weekly scheduled window for releasing new IMP software from one hour to two, now 7am to 9am Eastern on Tuesdays, because the network had grown to about forty IMPs. The window is always reserved even if not always used. It updates RFC 381 and RFC 406.

eli5.summary: The people fixing the network's machines used to need one hour each week. Now there were more machines, so they asked for two hours.

questions: how did network updates work in early arpanet
subtitle: Extending the ARPANET's weekly software update window from one to two hours.

tldr.problem: BBN needed to distribute new software to every IMP on the network, but as the network grew to about forty IMPs, one hour on Tuesday mornings was no longer sufficient time.
tldr.mechanism: BBN extended the regularly scheduled maintenance window from 7am to 8am to 7am to 9am Eastern Time, still on Tuesday mornings, to accommodate the growing network. Hosts receive advance notice via a type 2 IMP-to-Host message about an hour before the maintenance period.
tldr.outcome: The expanded window allows timely software updates as the network grows, though BBN acknowledged that linear scaling would eventually become impractical.

today: This RFC is part of ARPANET history, documenting early network operations and management. Modern networks use automatic, rolling updates deployed continuously rather than scheduled maintenance windows, making this centralized approach obsolete.

sections.title: Scheduled Maintenance
sections.content:
RFC 440 announces a change to the ARPANET's maintenance schedule. BBN, which managed the network's Interface Message Processors (IMPs), had established a regularly scheduled software maintenance period to minimize disruption: Tuesday mornings from 7am to 8am Eastern Time. During this hour, IMPs would receive updated software and host systems knew to expect downtime.

This approach, described in RFC 381, was designed to give the network community predictability: everyone knew when the network would be unavailable, rather than experiencing surprise downtime whenever a software update was needed.
sections.eli5: The network managers picked Tuesday mornings for maintenance so everyone would know when the network was going to be down.

sections.title: The Growing Network Problem
sections.content:
As the ARPANET expanded to about forty IMPs, the one-hour maintenance window became insufficient. Distributing new software to every IMP on the network was now taking longer than the reserved slot. Effective the first Tuesday in February 1973, BBN extended the scheduled maintenance window to two hours, from 7am to 9am Eastern Time.

The network still would not necessarily use the full window every week; it remained a reserved slot that was always available for maintenance, but only activated when needed. Hosts would receive advance notice via a type 2 IMP-to-Host message about an hour before a maintenance period was to begin.
sections.eli5: With more machines to update, they needed two hours instead of one on Tuesday mornings.

sections.title: Scaling Limitations
sections.content:
Walden's RFC acknowledges a fundamental problem: software maintenance cannot continue to scale linearly. If the one-hour window was barely enough for forty IMPs, and doubling to two hours was necessary, the arithmetic suggests that at some point a two-hour maintenance window would become too small as the network continued to grow.

The RFC expresses confidence that BBN would find a better solution before maintenance windows consumed an entire week of time. Indeed, future network growth would rely on new approaches to software distribution and update management, such as decentralized updates and rolling maintenance windows.
sections.eli5: The network leaders knew that this solution would not work forever if the network kept getting bigger.
